title: ETB or booster bundle: which fits your collection?
paragraphs: An Elite Trainer Box and a booster bundle can both contain packs, but they are different products. Start by deciding whether you want packs to open, accessories to use, or a particular sealed box to collect.

A booster bundle is generally the more focused pack purchase. For example, the official Journey Together booster bundle contains six packs. An ETB can include packs plus sleeves, accessories, a storage box, and a promo card. The regular Scarlet & Violet—151 ETB includes nine packs and a Snorlax promo. Check the specific product listing rather than applying those counts to every set or edition. [Journey Together bundle](https://www.pokemon.com/us/pokemon-tcg/product-gallery/scarlet-violet-journey-together-booster-bundle), [151 ETB](https://www.pokemon.com/us/pokemon-tcg/product-gallery/scarlet-violet-151-elite-trainer-box/)

If you mainly want packs, divide the complete purchase cost by the number of packs. In a hypothetical comparison, a six-pack bundle costing $36 works out to $6 per pack, while a nine-pack ETB costing $63 works out to $7 per pack. The ETB costs an additional $1 per pack in that example, with its other contents included in the purchase.

That comparison does not put a resale value on sleeves or a promo. If you want the accessories, compare what the whole purchase is worth to you. If you plan to keep the product sealed, the packaging and edition may matter more than the pack calculation.

Before choosing, check the set, language, edition, pack count, shipping charge, and whether the listing is factory sealed. Compare the exact versions in the catalog, then use the price-per-pack tool if opening packs is your main goal.
description: An Elite Trainer Box and a booster bundle can both contain packs, but they are different products.

title: Pokémon Center ETBs and regular ETBs
paragraphs: Two boxes can share the same expansion name and still be different collector products. A Pokémon Center Elite Trainer Box should be matched to its own listing when you compare prices.

Scarlet & Violet—151 provides a concrete example. The regular ETB has nine booster packs and a Snorlax promo. The Pokémon Center version has eleven booster packs and two Snorlax promos, one bearing a Pokémon Center logo. Those details describe this particular release; confirm the contents of each other set separately. [Regular 151 ETB](https://www.pokemon.com/us/pokemon-tcg/product-gallery/scarlet-violet-151-elite-trainer-box/), [Pokémon Center 151 ETB](https://www.pokemon.com/us/pokemon-tcg/product-gallery/scarlet-violet-151-pokemon-center-elite-trainer-box)

When comparing two listings, match the full product name, language, edition, and condition. Read the included-items list as well as looking at the box photograph. A listing for an empty display box, a removed promo, or an opened product is not the same purchase as a complete factory-sealed ETB.

If you intend to open the packs, compare the total price and the extras you actually want. If you collect sealed products, decide which edition belongs in your collection and use prices for that same edition. A higher asking price alone does not establish scarcity, demand, or future value.

Use the two product pages in PokeScratch side by side and check the date attached to each market snapshot. If a source or listing is unclear, resolve that mismatch before treating the price difference as a bargain.
description: Two boxes can share the same expansion name and still be different collector products.

title: How to compare Pokémon prices per pack
paragraphs: Price per pack answers a narrow question: how much of your total purchase cost are you paying for each included booster pack? It is useful when comparing products you plan to open.

Add the item price, shipping, and any tax amount you want to include. Subtract an applicable discount once. Divide that total by the pack count. Use the same approach for every product in the comparison.

Consider two hypothetical purchases. Product A costs $30 plus $6 shipping and includes six packs: $36 divided by six is $6 per pack. Product B costs $54 with shipping included and has nine packs: $54 divided by nine is also $6 per pack. The larger box has a higher checkout total, but the pack cost is the same.

Only compare equivalent packs when you want a direct cost comparison. A mixed-set collection box may contain packs you value differently, and packs in different languages are different purchases. The calculator should make those differences easier to notice, not erase them.

Do not automatically subtract a guessed resale price for accessories or promos. You might keep them, fail to sell them, or incur selling costs. Likewise, a low price per pack does not tell you what cards you will pull or what those cards will be worth.

Use the calculator with the actual listing’s pack count and checkout costs. For a mixed-set box, note which sets are included and decide whether you want every pack before comparing the average with a single-set bundle.
description: Compare the checkout cost of each booster pack, without guessing the value of accessories or pulls.

title: A checklist before buying sealed Pokémon online
paragraphs: A useful price comparison starts with making sure the listings describe the same thing. Check the full product name, set, language, edition, and number of items before comparing the totals.

Read the condition description. Is the listing for a factory-sealed product, an opened box with some contents removed, individual loose packs, or an empty box? A photograph can be reused, so inspect the written description and ask the seller to clarify an ambiguity before purchasing.

Next, compare the checkout cost rather than the headline number. Shipping, tax, and quantity can change which listing is cheaper. Read the seller’s return terms and the marketplace’s buyer-protection information for that specific purchase.

Be cautious about claims that cannot be established from a listing, including guaranteed valuable pulls or sweeping statements that a product is certain to rise in value. Packaging photos also cannot conclusively prove authenticity. Pokémon Support recommends becoming familiar with official packaging and consulting a knowledgeable local card shop when evaluating suspected counterfeits. [Pokémon Support](https://support.pokemon.com/hc/en-us/articles/360002068953-Did-I-purchase-fake-or-counterfeit-cards)

Use PokeScratch to identify the product and compare its dated reference information. Then check the actual retailer or marketplace listing for condition, availability, seller details, and the price you will pay. A reference value is not a reservation or a promise that a seller has stock.
Keep the order confirmation and the original listing details for your records. If something arrives incorrectly, contact the retailer or marketplace that handled the order.

title: Comparing a listing with a retail reference
paragraphs: A retail reference and a current seller’s price answer different questions. The first gives context for a product; the second tells you what that seller is asking for that listing now.

MSRP means manufacturer’s suggested retail price. A retailer’s observed price may be different. A marketplace estimate is another reference point, and it may describe a different time or a collection of transactions rather than an offer you can buy immediately. Read the source label and date attached to a number before comparing it.

Match the product first. A regular ETB and a Pokémon Center ETB are different editions. A single bundle and a multipack are different quantities. An opened box and a factory-sealed box are different conditions.

Then compare the full costs. In a hypothetical example, a product with a $50 retail reference is listed for $65 plus $5 shipping. The checkout cost before tax is $70, which is $20 above the reference. That is 40% above $50. This describes the difference; it does not tell you whether buying will be profitable.

A price above an older reference does not prove that the asking price is unreasonable. A price below a market snapshot does not guarantee a bargain. The source may be dated, the condition may differ, or the listing may have costs that are not included in the headline amount.

Use the references to ask better questions: Is this the exact edition? How recent is the comparison? What will I actually pay? Is the product and its condition worth that amount to me? If a detail looks wrong, send the product link and a source to hello@pokescratch.com.
